extraction.body: When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max raise the bar for performance in a phone with the new A20 Pro chip. You also get a versatile new variable aperture camera that takes brighter images and gives you more creative control. The battery life from both devices is awesome, too, and you get the fastest charging yet from an iPhone. You have to pay $100 more for both Pro phones, and they’re heavier than their predecessors, but overall these are easily the best phones money can buy. The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max don’t have a ‘wow’ feature to flex to your friends like the iPhone Duo. Yet beneath the familiar design is a pretty big leap forward for two areas people really care about: cameras and performance. With a new variable aperture main camera, the iPhone 18 Pro lets in more light and gives you more creative freedom than ever before with new Pro controls. And the A20 Pro chip — the first 2nm chip in an iPhone — delivers record-breaking speed that surpasses all Android flagships. Based on our testing, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max battery life is stellar, too. And with the new Siri AI on board these Pro phones are much more capable personal assistants. The bad news? The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are noticeably heavier than their predecessors, and the prices are $100 higher for both models. But if you’ve been putting off that upgrade for a while, you'll find that both of these Pros are the best phones you can buy. Here's all the pros and cons based on my in-depth testing in our full iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max review. 48MP main with variable aperture (f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, f/4), 48MP ultrawide (f/2.2), 48MP telephoto w/4x optical zoom (f/2.8) 48MP main with variable aperture (f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, f/4), 48MP ultrawide (f/2.2), 48MP telephoto w/4x optical zoom (f/2.8) The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for 256GB in the US, £1,199 in the UK, and AU$2,099 in Australia. That's $100 more than last year. Meanwhile, the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 / £1,299 / AU$2,299 for 256GB. You can upgrade to 512GB, 1TB, and 2TB of storage for both models. In terms of multi-core performance, the A20 Pro once again excelled, offering a 28% boost versus the iPhone 17 Pros. And we’re talking about a 10% advantage over the Galaxy S26 Ultra here. We also ran the newer Geekbench 7, which has a multi-core benchmark that’s designed to be more real-world and uses more challenging data sets. The iPhone 18 Pro delivered similar performance gains. The graphics leap is even more impressive from the A20 Pro. On the 3DMark Solar Bay Unlimited test, the iPhone 18 Pro turned in a frame rate of 62 fps, which is 33% faster than the 17 Pro. And the iPhone 18 Pro Max scored an even higher 67.9 fps, which is 45% faster than the 17 Pro Max. The Galaxy S26 Ultra just couldn’t keep up, as the regular iPhone 18 Pro was 25% faster and the iPhone 18 Pro Max was 37% higher. The iPhone 18 Pro Max turned in a stability score of 79.4%, which is 25% better than the iPhone 17 Pro Max. That’s also over 47% better than the Galaxy S26 Ultra. However, we saw only a minor 1.7% gain between the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro. Last but not least we tested AI performance using the Geekbench AI test. The iPhone 18 Pro turned in a Neural Engine score of 69,245 and the iPhone 18 Pro Max a much higher 71,974. That’s a boost of 41 to 48%, which means on-device AI tasks should run faster. Thanks to the efficiency of the A20 Pro chip and bigger batteries, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is rated to have the longest battery life ever of any iPhone. And the iPhone 18 Pro is rated for the endurance of last year’s iPhone 17 Pro Max, which made our best phone battery life list last year. The good news is that both the iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone 18 Pro last longer than their 17 Pro counterparts. But we didn’t see a huge leap in endurance. On the Tom’s Guide battery test, which involves continuous web surfing over 5G on 150 nits of screen brightness, the iPhone 18 Pro Max lasted 18 hours and 41 minutes on its longest run and averaged 18:27. The iPhone 17 Pro Max lasted 17:54. The iPhone 18 Pro lasted an average of 16:17 on our test, which is nearly an hour longer than the iPhone 17 Pro (15:21). The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have a first for iPhones, even though the Samsung Galaxy S9 tried it years ago. I’m talking about a variable aperture main camera. There’s six tiny blades inside the wide lens that can expand or contract depending on the conditions. For example, if you’re taking a portrait, the aperture might open up to f/1.48 to let in more light. And if you want more detail throughout the shot, the iPhone 18 Pro Max might stop down to f/4.0. This gives you more depth of field. The iPhone 18 Pro’s camera can do this all automatically, but there’s new Pro controls on board that lets you set the exact aperture with four options. When I captured a photo of begonias in Bryant Park, I selected f/1.48 to blur the background and f/4.0 to bring detail to the stage across the park and buildings. The wider aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max also enables the phones to let in significantly more light overall, which means better low-light images. Take this American flag photo captured in near darkness. You can make out more detail in the flag pole and the brick in the iPhone 18 Pro image. The Galaxy S26 Ultra shot is downright blurry. Indoors I’d give a slight edge to the iPhone 18 Pro with this shot of Halloween decorations. The dots of light reflecting off the transparent orb look sharper through the iPhone. But the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s photo has more saturated colors inside the ball and in the fabric. Other new features include 4K Timelapse in Dolby Vision HDR, higher-quality low-light video in 1080p resolution and Pro controls for video, such as shutter speed. To test out the iPhone 18 Pro’s video capabilities I shot this koi pond with a fountain using the new iPhone and Galaxy S26 Ultra at 4K at 30 fps with HDR turned on. I prefer the way the iPhone 18 Pro renders the details in the rocks and its smoother zooming motion; the S26 Ultra takes a second to regain focus. However, the S26 Ultra’s superior zoom shines when I get really close on the fountain wall. For example, I asked Siri to look up reviews for a hotel I was thinking of staying at with my brother for a road trip and send them via text in the same prompt. The results seemed okay but didn’t have as much detail as I’d like. So I tried again, asking for best dishes. I can also control three different apps with the same prompt, such as setting a reminder, starting a timer and looking up photos and adding them to a Note. The new Siri AI is smarter and more powerful, but sometimes it started doing the first thing I asked before I got to the second request, interrupting the flow. Visual Intelligence also gets an upgrade with iOS 27 and the iPhone 18 Pros. For example, I pointed the iPhone 18 Pro Max at a flyer with a bunch of dates on it, and it automatically recognized the dates and asked if I wanted to add them to my calendar. I especially like that there’s a dedicated Siri mode in the camera app so you don’t have to go to a separate app. Perhaps owing to the bigger batteries, variable aperture lens camera and larger vapor chambers, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are heftier than their predecessors despite having the same dimensions as before. In terms of multi-core performance, the A20 Pro once again excelled, offering a 28% boost versus the iPhone 17 Pros. And we’re talking about a 10% advantage over the Galaxy S26 Ultra here.

passages: The short version of that first piece is that phone sensors are tiny and permanently starved for light, so stopping down is the last thing you want to do, and depth of field on a phone is already so deep that Apple has spent years writing software to fake the blur a real lens would give you.
Every other phone that has shipped a variable aperture uses it wide open in the dark, accepts that wide open is soft, and stops down the rest of the time.
So the variable aperture is a cool feature and I am going to enjoy using it.
Here is that translation in one place, every aperture the new phone can reach next to the full frame f-stop that would blur the background by the same amount.
My camera was at ISO 100, the lowest native setting on both my camera and the iPhone, and 1/50 of a second, which is the shutter speed everyone in those comments is chasing.

extraction.body: Four days ago I put out a very nerdy video about the variable aperture lens in the new iPhone 18 Pro , and it has since become the most watched thing I have made all year. I did not see that coming. What I really did not see coming was the comment section. A lot of you disagreed with me, at length, and told me I had missed the point entirely. So I went back through every one of those arguments. I still think you are wrong, and this time I went outside and measured it. The short version of that first piece is that phone sensors are tiny and permanently starved for light, so stopping down is the last thing you want to do, and depth of field on a phone is already so deep that Apple has spent years writing software to fake the blur a real lens would give you. Every other phone that has shipped a variable aperture uses it wide open in the dark, accepts that wide open is soft, and stops down the rest of the time. Once you have built a mechanism that moves at all, you may as well let it run to f/4. Start with the equation, because most of the arguments in that comment section fall apart on it. The f-number is the focal length divided by the diameter of the entrance pupil. You have probably seen the main camera described as a 24mm. Run the math backwards with that number and at f/1.48 the entrance pupil would have to be roughly 17 millimeters across, which is wider than the entire camera module sitting on the back of the phone. Obviously not. The iPhone does not have a 24mm lens. It has a 24mm equivalent field of view, meaning that if you put a 24mm lens on a full frame body you would frame up roughly the same shot. The actual focal length is about 7 millimeters. Do the division properly and the entrance pupil wide open is about 4.7 millimeters. That is the real hole the light goes through. This is the part people keep tripping over. Shutter speed, ISO and f-stop are universal. Dial the same three into an iPhone and into a professional camera and you should get the same exposure, because those numbers describe light per unit of sensor area. Pick any equivalent patch out of either sensor and the same amount of light is landing on it. What changes is everything downstream. A full frame sensor has roughly 12 times the area, so it needs 12 times the total light for the same exposure, which demands a far wider entrance pupil, and a wider entrance pupil is precisely what produces shallow depth of field. The exposure numbers transfer between cameras. The look does not. Here is that translation in one place, every aperture the new phone can reach next to the full frame f-stop that would blur the background by the same amount. Wide open at f/1.48, the phone is giving you roughly what f/5.2 looks like on a full frame body. Stop it down to f/4 and you are somewhere around f/14. That is the entire reason a phone photo looks like a phone photo, and it is why no amount of variable aperture is going to hand you background blur. Here is the detail I left out last time, and it answers a question several of you asked. If f-stops really are universal, why does the iPhone stop at f/4 instead of running all the way to f/22 like a proper lens? Diffraction. Every lens has it, variable aperture or not. As the entrance pupil gets smaller, light bends around the edge of the opening and images start going soft, which is why no lens is at its sharpest at its smallest aperture. It bites phones much harder than it bites professional cameras, and not because phone sensors are small. It is because their photosites are. The Sony a7S III I shoot myself on is a full frame camera with 12 megapixels, so each individual pixel is enormous. The iPhone crams 48 megapixels onto a sensor a small fraction of that size. Apple could not offer you f/11 or f/22 even if they wanted to. The files would come back visibly blurry. The single most upvoted complaint, across several comments with hundreds of thumbs up each, was some version of this: you are missing the point, this was never a photo feature, Apple built it for videographers. Being able to stop down to f/4 finally lets you hold a 180 degree shutter at 1/48 of a second and get natural motion blur, which has always been the hard part of shooting video on a phone. If that means nothing to you: photographers can shoot at almost any shutter speed, because a still image is a still image. Videographers want a little blur baked into every frame. Shake your hand in front of a camera running at 1/48 and freeze it, and the hand smears slightly, which is what your eye reads as natural motion. Use a much faster shutter and the footage goes jittery and strange. Nearly every movie and TV show you have ever watched was shot this way, and it is one of the first things we cover in Introduction to Video . It is a reasonable theory. It is also the easiest claim here to test. The day I shot this was overcast with a storm cloud parked in front of the sun, which is about as dark as daylight gets. Best case scenario for the argument. My camera was at ISO 100, the lowest native setting on both my camera and the iPhone, and 1/50 of a second, which is the shutter speed everyone in those comments is chasing. To get a correct exposure I had to be at f/8. Open that up to f/4, the widest the iPhone can go while still being stopped down, and the same shot is two stops overexposed. The zebras take over the frame. You can argue that the iPhone drops to ISO 50, so I tested that too. Still overexposed. And remember the storm cloud. Shoot in direct sunlight and you are another three or four stops brighter than the day I was standing in. So if you were hoping to buy this phone, stop down to f/4 and shoot at 1/48 all day outdoors, I am sorry. On a professional lens you could keep going to f/11 or f/22 and eventually land on it. The iPhone stops at f/4, so outside you are still reaching for a neutral density filter , which is basically sunglasses for your camera. Normally I would laugh at the whole exercise and tell you it is an iPhone, the shutter speed does not have to be perfect, the footage will look fine straight out of the camera. But Apple has built a real set of manual controls into the camera app this year, and I can genuinely imagine reaching for them now. So the variable aperture is a cool feature and I am going to enjoy using it. Just do not let anyone convince you it is about to transform your photography or your video work. It is another small step forward, and not much more than that. My full review goes up once the phone actually lands. Unrelated to any of the above: I have been building a Mac app called Better Dock for years, and the beta is finally open. It replaces the dock at the bottom of macOS with something you can actually configure, and if you run several monitors like I do, you can put a dock on every screen and see exactly what is open where. It is free to try at betterdockapp.com, and there will always be a free version. Lee Morris is a professional photographer based in Charleston SC, and is the co-owner of Fstoppers.com

coreStoryFacts.text: Photographer Tyler Stalman is back with his annual iPhone camera review.
Here’s what he had to say about the iPhone 18 Pro’s new variable aperture, photographic styles, Apple Reference Image, and more.
As for his impressions, he says Soft Skin does a subtle job of reducing skin detail without simply blurring it, while Glow adds a diffused highlight effect similar to a black mist filter.
Stalman notes that although he enjoyed last year’s Cosmic Orange color on his iPhone 17 Pro, it tended to appear in reflections when shooting through windows.
For this reason, he says pro photographers might want to stick to Burgundy or Black, as they are less likely to cast unwanted color into photos or videos.

This part of the review includes a few very cool-looking shots of the iris mechanism opening and closing, and Stalman points out that Apple’s implementation is somewhat unusual, with the aperture blades positioned above the primary lens element rather than deeper inside the lens, as they typically are on traditional camera lenses.

extraction.body: Photographer Tyler Stalman is back with his annual iPhone camera review. Here’s what he had to say about the iPhone 18 Pro’s new variable aperture, photographic styles, Apple Reference Image, and more. Although this year’s iPhone 18 Pro introduces many new features, including the 2nm A20 Pro chip, a new vapor chamber, and a smaller Dynamic Island, it is fair to say that the biggest camera upgrade is its new variable aperture system. Also new this year are updates to Cinematic mode, expanded Photographic Styles with new texture controls, Apple Reference Image, and further improvements to the Camera app’s pro controls. Today, photographer Tyler Stalman published a review of all of the iPhone 18 Pro’s new hardware and software features, adding to the wave of reviews that went live as the embargo lifted, including ours . Stalman notes that although he enjoyed last year’s Cosmic Orange color on his iPhone 17 Pro, it tended to appear in reflections when shooting through windows. For this reason, he says pro photographers might want to stick to Burgundy or Black, as they are less likely to cast unwanted color into photos or videos. He also notes right off the bat that his review compares the iPhone 18 Pro’s cameras to those of the iPhone 15 Pro, while the video itself was shot almost entirely on an iPhone 17 Pro. When it comes to the main camera upgrade, which is the new variable aperture, Stalman says its addition is “one step along the way to making (the iPhone) a serious camera.” He also notes that the wider f/1.48 aperture lets more light reach the sensor, which can help keep ISO lower in low-light conditions and reduce the need for Night mode. This part of the review includes a few very cool-looking shots of the iris mechanism opening and closing, and Stalman points out that Apple’s implementation is somewhat unusual, with the aperture blades positioned above the primary lens element rather than deeper inside the lens, as they typically are on traditional camera lenses. Stalman also says that the iPhone 18 Pro’s 4x zoom (also present in last year’s iPhone) is a nice improvement over the iPhone 16 Pro’s 5x zoom, which could at times feel a little too tight. And speaking of going too far, he quickly touches on the new AI-powered editing tools, such as Clean Up, Extend, and Reframe, noting that although they are technically impressive and quite convincing, they can make such significant changes that the resulting image no longer feels entirely authentic to the original photo. When it comes to the iPhone 18 Pro’s new texture options, including Soft Skin, Glow, and Film, Stalman demonstrates each effect by moving its intensity from 0 to 100. As for his impressions, he says Soft Skin does a subtle job of reducing skin detail without simply blurring it, while Glow adds a diffused highlight effect similar to a black mist filter. He is also impressed by the Film effect’s grain and halation, though he wishes Apple offered more control over the amount of grain. The review also touches on Apple Reference Image , the iPhone’s Cinematic mode (and how Stalman still recommends Apple Log for truly cinematic footage), as well as the new Apple Log 2, and is naturally peppered with photo and video comparisons between the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro. Once you’re done, make sure you catch 9to5Mac’s own review of the iPhone 18 Pro , which also includes multiple photo comparisons between the new device and the iPhone 17 Pro. FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More. Check out 9to5Mac on YouTube for more Apple news: Marcus Mendes is a Brazilian tech podcaster and journalist who has been closely following Apple since the mid-2000s.

Every other phone that has shipped a variable aperture uses it wide open in the dark, accepts that wide open is soft, and stops down the rest of the time.

So the variable aperture is a cool feature and I am going to enjoy using it. Here is that translation in one place, every aperture the new phone can reach next to the full frame f-stop that would blur the background by the same amount. extraction.body: Four days ago I put out a very nerdy video about the variable aperture lens in the new iPhone 18 Pro , and it has since become the most watched thing I have made all year. I did not see that coming. What I really did not see coming was the comment section. A lot of you disagreed with me, at length, and told me I had missed the point entirely. So I went back through every one of those arguments. I still think you are wrong, and this time I went outside and measured it. The short version of that first piece is that phone sensors are tiny and permanently starved for light, so stopping down is the last thing you want to do, and depth of field on a phone is already so deep that Apple has spent years writing software to fake the blur a real lens would give you. Every other phone that has shipped a variable aperture uses it wide open in the dark, accepts that wide open is soft, and stops down the rest of the time. Once you have built a mechanism that moves at all, you may as well let it run to f/4. Start with the equation, because most of the arguments in that comment section fall apart on it. The f-number is the focal length divided by the diameter of the entrance pupil. You have probably seen the main camera described as a 24mm. Run the math backwards with that number and at f/1.48 the entrance pupil would have to be roughly 17 millimeters across, which is wider than the entire camera module sitting on the back of the phone. Obviously not. The iPhone does not have a 24mm lens. It has a 24mm equivalent field of view, meaning that if you put a 24mm lens on a full frame body you would frame up roughly the same shot. The actual focal length is about 7 millimeters. Do the division properly and the entrance pupil wide open is about 4.7 millimeters. That is the real hole the light goes through. This is the part people keep tripping over. Shutter speed, ISO and f-stop are universal. Dial the same three into an iPhone and into a professional camera and you should get the same exposure, because those numbers describe light per unit of sensor area. Pick any equivalent patch out of either sensor and the same amount of light is landing on it. What changes is everything downstream. A full frame sensor has roughly 12 times the area, so it needs 12 times the total light for the same exposure, which demands a far wider entrance pupil, and a wider entrance pupil is precisely what produces shallow depth of field. The exposure numbers transfer between cameras. The look does not. Here is that translation in one place, every aperture the new phone can reach next to the full frame f-stop that would blur the background by the same amount. Wide open at f/1.48, the phone is giving you roughly what f/5.2 looks like on a full frame body. Stop it down to f/4 and you are somewhere around f/14. That is the entire reason a phone photo looks like a phone photo, and it is why no amount of variable aperture is going to hand you background blur. Here is the detail I left out last time, and it answers a question several of you asked. If f-stops really are universal, why does the iPhone stop at f/4 instead of running all the way to f/22 like a proper lens? Diffraction. Every lens has it, variable aperture or not. As the entrance pupil gets smaller, light bends around the edge of the opening and images start going soft, which is why no lens is at its sharpest at its smallest aperture. It bites phones much harder than it bites professional cameras, and not because phone sensors are small. It is because their photosites are. The Sony a7S III I shoot myself on is a full frame camera with 12 megapixels, so each individual pixel is enormous. The iPhone crams 48 megapixels onto a sensor a small fraction of that size. Apple could not offer you f/11 or f/22 even if they wanted to. The files would come back visibly blurry. The single most upvoted complaint, across several comments with hundreds of thumbs up each, was some version of this: you are missing the point, this was never a photo feature, Apple built it for videographers. Being able to stop down to f/4 finally lets you hold a 180 degree shutter at 1/48 of a second and get natural motion blur, which has always been the hard part of shooting video on a phone. If that means nothing to you: photographers can shoot at almost any shutter speed, because a still image is a still image. Videographers want a little blur baked into every frame. Shake your hand in front of a camera running at 1/48 and freeze it, and the hand smears slightly, which is what your eye reads as natural motion. Use a much faster shutter and the footage goes jittery and strange. Nearly every movie and TV show you have ever watched was shot this way, and it is one of the first things we cover in Introduction to Video . It is a reasonable theory. It is also the easiest claim here to test. The day I shot this was overcast with a storm cloud parked in front of the sun, which is about as dark as daylight gets. Best case scenario for the argument. My camera was at ISO 100, the lowest native setting on both my camera and the iPhone, and 1/50 of a second, which is the shutter speed everyone in those comments is chasing. To get a correct exposure I had to be at f/8. Open that up to f/4, the widest the iPhone can go while still being stopped down, and the same shot is two stops overexposed. The zebras take over the frame. You can argue that the iPhone drops to ISO 50, so I tested that too. Still overexposed. And remember the storm cloud. Shoot in direct sunlight and you are another three or four stops brighter than the day I was standing in. So if you were hoping to buy this phone, stop down to f/4 and shoot at 1/48 all day outdoors, I am sorry. On a professional lens you could keep going to f/11 or f/22 and eventually land on it. The iPhone stops at f/4, so outside you are still reaching for a neutral density filter , which is basically sunglasses for your camera. Normally I would laugh at the whole exercise and tell you it is an iPhone, the shutter speed does not have to be perfect, the footage will look fine straight out of the camera. But Apple has built a real set of manual controls into the camera app this year, and I can genuinely imagine reaching for them now. So the variable aperture is a cool feature and I am going to enjoy using it. Just do not let anyone convince you it is about to transform your photography or your video work. It is another small step forward, and not much more than that. My full review goes up once the phone actually lands. Unrelated to any of the above: I have been building a Mac app called Better Dock for years, and the beta is finally open. It replaces the dock at the bottom of macOS with something you can actually configure, and if you run several monitors like I do, you can put a dock on every screen and see exactly what is open where. It is free to try at betterdockapp.com, and there will always be a free version. Lee Morris is a professional photographer based in Charleston SC, and is the co-owner of Fstoppers.com

story.title: These camera apps give you more control over the iPhone 18 Pro’s aperture

facts.text: Photographer Tyler Stalman is back with his annual iPhone camera review.
Here’s what he had to say about the iPhone 18 Pro’s new variable aperture, photographic styles, Apple Reference Image, and more.
As for his impressions, he says Soft Skin does a subtle job of reducing skin detail without simply blurring it, while Glow adds a diffused highlight effect similar to a black mist filter.
Stalman notes that although he enjoyed last year’s Cosmic Orange color on his iPhone 17 Pro, it tended to appear in reflections when shooting through windows.
For this reason, he says pro photographers might want to stick to Burgundy or Black, as they are less likely to cast unwanted color into photos or videos.

This part of the review includes a few very cool-looking shots of the iris mechanism opening and closing, and Stalman points out that Apple’s implementation is somewhat unusual, with the aperture blades positioned above the primary lens element rather than deeper inside the lens, as they typically are on traditional camera lenses.

The iPhoneographers YouTube channel tested the new functionality in version 3.5 of the app last week and while they describe it as “pretty buggy” the app has since been updated to version 3.5.1 with “general performance and stability improvements.” Yesterday, Moment followed suit with an announcement on X that its $12.99 Moment Pro Camera II app has also been updated to support the iPhone 18 Pro’s variable aperture.
Apple’s SDK allows third-party camera apps to implement more granular control of the aperture.
You can adjust the aperture from f/1.48 to f/4.0 in 1/3 stop increments giving you 10 presets like Blackmagic’s app, which is the same approach as most digital cameras take.
My take on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max is that they are obscenely powerful phones inside a quiet redesign.
You get the fastest chip ever in a phone with the A20 Pro, a variable aperture camera I find easy to use and overdue Pro controls that give you more creative freedom when shooting photos and videos.
You have to pay $100 more for both Pro phones, and they’re heavier than their predecessors, but overall these are easily the best phones money can buy.
And with the new Siri AI on board these Pro phones are much more capable personal assistants.
At least they fit in the same cases as the 17 Pro series if you're upgrading.

But we didn’t see a huge leap in endurance.

It’s the better choice for watching videos and multitasking.

The dots of light reflecting off the transparent orb look sharper through the iPhone.

extraction.body: Apple is expected to announce more hardware before the end of the year following the debut of the iPhone 18 Pro and folding iPhone Duo earlier this month. The updated products will include a new version of the HomePod mini, the iPad mini 8, and the Apple TV 4K, according to details and images discovered in Apple’s own code by MacRumors contributor Aaron Perris. Details from the leaks are sparse, but the HomePod Mini 2 will carry forward a similar design to the original model that debuted in late 2020. While the current model is available in bright color options including orange, yellow, and blue, the leaked images of the HomePod Mini 2 reveal new green, pink, blue, white, and black shades that are more subdued and better suited to blending into existing decor. The new iPad mini 8 will replace the seventh-generation model that launched two years ago with an upgrade from Apple’s A17 Pro chip to the recently announced A20 Pro found in the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max, and iPhone Duo. The leaked images only show the front of the iPad mini 8, but Apple has moved its front-facing camera to the landscape edge of the tablet, while a groove on the top edge of the display, similar to the iPhone’s, seems to indicate an added speaker. As previously reported by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the next version of the iPad could also include improved waterproofing thanks to a new vibration-based speaker, and an OLED display like the larger iPad Pro features. The current version of the Apple TV is nearly four years old, but today’s leaks don’t give much away about what upgrades the new 4th generation version will include aside from a very similar design to its predecessor. Previous details uncovered by MacRumors’ Perris include a potential upgrade to Apple’s A17 Pro chip, while in 2024 Mark Gurman said the next Apple TV would use Apple’s in-house Bluetooth and Wi-Fi chip we now know as the N1.

Many previous rumors have suggested that the next mini tablet will be the iPad mini with OLED, meant to launch this October. Just because OLED doesn't appear in the code doesn't mean that it won't launch this fall though.
That said, the iPad mini running the A20 Pro chip is new and should make Apple's smallest tablet quite powerful. For instance, the iPad mini 7 , released two years ago features an A17 Pro chipset.

It appears that new version of the HomePod mini will be released in five colors which appear to include white, black, green, blue and a pinkish variant. The current models come in blue, yellow, orange, midnight and white.

We've tracked the HomePod mini 2 on our rumor radar since at least 2023 . It should be a simple update including a new chip that will likely let it run Apple Intelligence and Siri AI as with every other device listed above. It's also expected to have improved audio.
We expect all four devices to launch before the end of October alongside the HomePad smart home hub, and new M6 Macbooks.

extraction.body: Apple is expected to announce more hardware before the end of the year following the debut of the iPhone 18 Pro and folding iPhone Duo earlier this month. The updated products will include a new version of the HomePod mini, the iPad mini 8, and the Apple TV 4K, according to details and images discovered in Apple’s own code by MacRumors contributor Aaron Perris. Details from the leaks are sparse, but the HomePod Mini 2 will carry forward a similar design to the original model that debuted in late 2020. While the current model is available in bright color options including orange, yellow, and blue, the leaked images of the HomePod Mini 2 reveal new green, pink, blue, white, and black shades that are more subdued and better suited to blending into existing decor. The new iPad mini 8 will replace the seventh-generation model that launched two years ago with an upgrade from Apple’s A17 Pro chip to the recently announced A20 Pro found in the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max, and iPhone Duo. The leaked images only show the front of the iPad mini 8, but Apple has moved its front-facing camera to the landscape edge of the tablet, while a groove on the top edge of the display, similar to the iPhone’s, seems to indicate an added speaker. As previously reported by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the next version of the iPad could also include improved waterproofing thanks to a new vibration-based speaker, and an OLED display like the larger iPad Pro features. The current version of the Apple TV is nearly four years old, but today’s leaks don’t give much away about what upgrades the new 4th generation version will include aside from a very similar design to its predecessor. Previous details uncovered by MacRumors’ Perris include a potential upgrade to Apple’s A17 Pro chip, while in 2024 Mark Gurman said the next Apple TV would use Apple’s in-house Bluetooth and Wi-Fi chip we now know as the N1.

sources.title: Anthropic to pay Akamai $11.6 billion over seven years in cloud deal
passages: Anthropic will spend $11.6 billion over seven years on Akamai’s cloud infrastructure, Akamai said Thursday .
That’s more than six times the size of a $1.8 billion deal between the two companies that Bloomberg reported in May.

As part of the deal, Akamai issued Anthropic a warrant, essentially the right to buy shares at a set price, for nonvoting preferred stock convertible into 7.7 million common shares, or up to about 5% of the company’s outstanding stock, at $111.33 a share.
About 2% is expected to vest, or become available to Anthropic once it makes its first payment under the deal.
It also represents a bet on a less-hyped corner of AI infrastructure: CPUs.

Demand for CPUs, the general-purpose chips that handle work like running code and browsing the web, has grown as AI agents take on more tasks, though Akamai didn’t say what Anthropic will use them for.
The warrant flips the more common pattern in circular AI deals , in which suppliers — chipmakers and cloud providers — invest directly in the AI labs that buy their products.
Here, the supplier is instead giving its customer a potential stake, one that grows as Anthropic’s spending with Akamai does.
AMD used a similar structure with OpenAI last year, tying warrants to chip-purchase milestones.
Akamai won’t see revenue from the deal this year.

On an investor call Thursday, executives said they expect $150 million to $300 million in 2027, starting in the second half, with revenue reaching an annual pace of about $1.7 billion by the end of 2028.
To build out the capacity, Akamai expects to spend about $5.5 billion.
Anthropic is no stranger to such arrangements.
Amazon , Google , Microsoft, and AMD have all invested or agreed to invest in the company while selling it chips or cloud capacity.
CEO Dario Amodei told The New York Times last December that Anthropic does not participate in these deals at the “same scale as some other players.”
Akamai shares rose as much as 17% in after-hours trading on Thursday, The Wall Street Journal reported .

sources.title: Akamai Shares Surge 20% After Signing $11.6 Billion, Seven-Year Cloud Deal With Anthropic - finance.biggo.com
passages: The vesting schedule is tied directly to Anthropic's spending commitments.
Stock equal to roughly 2% of Akamai's outstanding shares is expected to vest because of the initial $11.6 billion commitment announced Thursday.
The remaining approximately 3% would vest through the successful expansion of the commitment up to an additional $9 billion within the seven-year warrant period.
Shares climbed to $130 in late trading, reflecting investor enthusiasm for a deal that could reshape Akamai's growth trajectory over the next several years.
The agreement also gives Anthropic a path to own nearly 5% of Akamai as cloud spending expands.
For investors, the equity warrant structure adds an intriguing dimension to the deal.
The structure also provides Akamai with a degree of revenue visibility that extends well beyond the initial seven-year term, assuming Anthropic exercises its expansion options.
A 20% single-day surge in after-hours trading reflects not just the immediate revenue implications but also the strategic positioning the company has achieved in the AI infrastructure landscape.
With capital expenditures projected to rise significantly in 2026, Akamai is betting that the long-term payoff from hosting Anthropic's workloads will justify the upfront investment.

The contract, which supports Anthropic's CPU workload requirements through Akamai Cloud's distributed AI infrastructure and software, adds to more than $2.8 billion in multiyear Cloud Infrastructure Services commitments Akamai had already announced from other customers this year.
The financial commitment required to support the contract is substantial.
The company also anticipates roughly $1.7 billion in additional capital spending during 2026, with some funds directed toward securing critical hardware ahead of time.
Akamai intends to pre-buy supply chain components, including memory, before the need for increased computing power arises.
Beyond the computing capacity, the two companies structured an equity component into the arrangement.
Anthropic entered the year with an unusually large private-market valuation, having raised $65 billion in May at a $965 billion post-money valuation.
The Akamai deal underscores the intensifying competition among cloud and infrastructure providers to capture business from leading AI developers.

For Akamai, traditionally known for content delivery and security services, the Anthropic contract represents a significant expansion into the high-growth AI infrastructure segment that has propelled rivals like Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud to record revenues.
The proposal would create a separate class of shares for the seven founders, allowing them to vote together on most major corporate matters.

As the AI arms race continues to accelerate, infrastructure providers capable of delivering secure, scalable computing capacity at competitive prices are emerging as critical enablers of the technology's growth.
Tom Leighton framed the partnership as validation of the company's infrastructure capabilities.
Anthropic is also contemplating the introduction of another special class of stock aimed at giving employee shares the role of breaking corporate vote ties.
The announcement comes as Anthropic is simultaneously restructuring its corporate governance ahead of a possible initial public offering.
The Information reported Thursday that Anthropic wants shareholders to approve a structure that would give CEO Dario Amodei and his six co-founders 50.1% of total voting power.

The proposed governance structure draws parallels to the system used by Peter Thiel at Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR), where founders retain special voting rights to ensure control despite ownership dilution.
Despite the scale of the deal, Akamai does not expect the new contract to affect its 2026 revenue guidance.
The governance overhaul is being introduced as Anthropic prepares for what could become one of the largest IPOs ever.
The Claude developer could wait until after the U.S. midterm elections in November before moving forward with the offering.
Reuters reported earlier this month that the election itself is not expected to have a major effect on the IPO process.

That’s more than six times the size of a $1.8 billion deal between the two companies that Bloomberg reported in May.

As part of the deal, Akamai issued Anthropic a warrant, essentially the right to buy shares at a set price, for nonvoting preferred stock convertible into 7.7 million common shares, or up to about 5% of the company’s outstanding stock, at $111.33 a share.
About 2% is expected to vest, or become available to Anthropic once it makes its first payment under the deal.
It also represents a bet on a less-hyped corner of AI infrastructure: CPUs.

Demand for CPUs, the general-purpose chips that handle work like running code and browsing the web, has grown as AI agents take on more tasks, though Akamai didn’t say what Anthropic will use them for.
The warrant flips the more common pattern in circular AI deals , in which suppliers — chipmakers and cloud providers — invest directly in the AI labs that buy their products.

AMD used a similar structure with OpenAI last year, tying warrants to chip-purchase milestones.
Akamai won’t see revenue from the deal this year.

To build out the capacity, Akamai expects to spend about $5.5 billion.
Anthropic is no stranger to such arrangements.
Amazon , Google , Microsoft, and AMD have all invested or agreed to invest in the company while selling it chips or cloud capacity.
CEO Dario Amodei told The New York Times last December that Anthropic does not participate in these deals at the “same scale as some other players.”
Akamai shares rose as much as 17% in after-hours trading on Thursday, The Wall Street Journal reported .

The remaining approximately 3% would vest through the successful expansion of the commitment up to an additional $9 billion within the seven-year warrant period.

The agreement also gives Anthropic a path to own nearly 5% of Akamai as cloud spending expands.
For investors, the equity warrant structure adds an intriguing dimension to the deal.
The structure also provides Akamai with a degree of revenue visibility that extends well beyond the initial seven-year term, assuming Anthropic exercises its expansion options.
A 20% single-day surge in after-hours trading reflects not just the immediate revenue implications but also the strategic positioning the company has achieved in the AI infrastructure landscape.

passages: Anthropic will spend $11.6 billion over seven years on Akamai’s cloud infrastructure, Akamai said Thursday .
That’s more than six times the size of a $1.8 billion deal between the two companies that Bloomberg reported in May.

About 2% is expected to vest, or become available to Anthropic once it makes its first payment under the deal.
It also represents a bet on a less-hyped corner of AI infrastructure: CPUs.

The warrant flips the more common pattern in circular AI deals , in which suppliers — chipmakers and cloud providers — invest directly in the AI labs that buy their products.

To build out the capacity, Akamai expects to spend about $5.5 billion.
Anthropic is no stranger to such arrangements.
Amazon , Google , Microsoft, and AMD have all invested or agreed to invest in the company while selling it chips or cloud capacity.

extraction.body: Akamai Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ: AKAM) saw its stock rocket as much as 20% in extended trading on Thursday after the company disclosed a massive seven-year computing agreement with Anthropic PBC valued at $11.6 billion, with provisions that could push the total beyond $20 billion. The contract, which supports Anthropic's CPU workload requirements through Akamai Cloud's distributed AI infrastructure and software, adds to more than $2.8 billion in multiyear Cloud Infrastructure Services commitments Akamai had already announced from other customers this year. Those existing deals cover infrastructure used to build, launch, and run large AI workloads, positioning the Cambridge, Massachusetts-based company as a growing force in the artificial intelligence infrastructure market. Shares climbed to $130 in late trading, reflecting investor enthusiasm for a deal that could reshape Akamai's growth trajectory over the next several years. The agreement also gives Anthropic a path to own nearly 5% of Akamai as cloud spending expands. Beyond the computing capacity, the two companies structured an equity component into the arrangement. Akamai issued Anthropic a warrant tied to a potential stake in the company. The warrant covers non-voting convertible Series B preferred stock equal to 7.7 million Akamai common shares after conversion. If fully exercised, the position would represent approximately 5% of Akamai's outstanding common stock, with an exercise price of $111.33 per common share. The vesting schedule is tied directly to Anthropic's spending commitments. Stock equal to roughly 2% of Akamai's outstanding shares is expected to vest because of the initial $11.6 billion commitment announced Thursday. The remaining approximately 3% would vest through the successful expansion of the commitment up to an additional $9 billion within the seven-year warrant period. Each additional $3 billion purchase of cloud services under terms agreed by both companies would unlock another amount equal to about 1% of Akamai's outstanding common shares. Akamai co-founder and CEO Dr. Tom Leighton framed the partnership as validation of the company's infrastructure capabilities. "Anthropic is advancing the AI revolution and we are thrilled they chose Akamai's capabilities for building and operating AI infrastructure at scale," he said. He added that Akamai's global network and experience working with large companies put it in position to handle AI applications and workloads that require security and large amounts of computing capacity. The financial commitment required to support the contract is substantial. Akamai expects to spend approximately $5.5 billion in capital expenditures related to the original $11.6 billion commitment. The company also anticipates roughly $1.7 billion in additional capital spending during 2026, with some funds directed toward securing critical hardware ahead of time. Akamai intends to pre-buy supply chain components, including memory, before the need for increased computing power arises. Despite the scale of the deal, Akamai does not expect the new contract to affect its 2026 revenue guidance. The announcement comes as Anthropic is simultaneously restructuring its corporate governance ahead of a possible initial public offering. The Information reported Thursday that Anthropic wants shareholders to approve a structure that would give CEO Dario Amodei and his six co-founders 50.1% of total voting power. The proposal would create a separate class of shares for the seven founders, allowing them to vote together on most major corporate matters. The arrangement would continue as long as at least three of the seven founders maintain a required minimum amount of Anthropic shares. The proposed governance structure draws parallels to the system used by Peter Thiel at Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR), where founders retain special voting rights to ensure control despite ownership dilution. One notable restriction: the special voting rights would not apply to board elections for Anthropic, which currently has seven board seats with one seat unoccupied. Anthropic is also contemplating the introduction of another special class of stock aimed at giving employee shares the role of breaking corporate vote ties. The governance overhaul is being introduced as Anthropic prepares for what could become one of the largest IPOs ever. The Claude developer could wait until after the U.S. midterm elections in November before moving forward with the offering. Reuters reported earlier this month that the election itself is not expected to have a major effect on the IPO process. Anthropic entered the year with an unusually large private-market valuation, having raised $65 billion in May at a $965 billion post-money valuation. The Akamai deal underscores the intensifying competition among cloud and infrastructure providers to capture business from leading AI developers. For Akamai, traditionally known for content delivery and security services, the Anthropic contract represents a significant expansion into the high-growth AI infrastructure segment that has propelled rivals like Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud to record revenues. For investors, the equity warrant structure adds an intriguing dimension to the deal. By tying stock vesting to Anthropic's incremental spending, Akamai has effectively created a mechanism that aligns the interests of both companies while giving Anthropic an incentive to deepen its commitment over time. The structure also provides Akamai with a degree of revenue visibility that extends well beyond the initial seven-year term, assuming Anthropic exercises its expansion options. The market's enthusiastic response to the announcement suggests investors see the deal as a transformative event for Akamai. A 20% single-day surge in after-hours trading reflects not just the immediate revenue implications but also the strategic positioning the company has achieved in the AI infrastructure landscape. With capital expenditures projected to rise significantly in 2026, Akamai is betting that the long-term payoff from hosting Anthropic's workloads will justify the upfront investment. As the AI arms race continues to accelerate, infrastructure providers capable of delivering secure, scalable computing capacity at competitive prices are emerging as critical enablers of the technology's growth. Akamai's ability to secure a marquee customer like Anthropic — one of the most valuable private companies in the world — signals that its distributed cloud architecture may offer advantages that traditional hyperscalers cannot easily replicate. sources.title: Anthropic to get up to 5% Akamai stake in $11.6 billion cloud deal
passages: Anthropic is set to get a warrant for up to a 5% stake in Akamai Technologies as part of an expanded seven-year cloud infrastructure agreement worth $11.6 billion, as the AI company continues to secure computing capacity to support the growing demands of its models.

Under the agreement announced by Akamai on September 24, Anthropic will receive a warrant to purchase non-voting convertible Series B preferred stock representing 7.7 million Akamai shares on an as-converted basis, or up to approximately 5% of Akamai’s common stock outstanding.
Akamai shares rose 22% in extended trading following the announcement, reflecting investor reaction to the size and duration of the Anthropic commitment.
The deal can expand to as much as $20 billion if Anthropic takes up the additional $9 billion in capacity.

According to media reports, Anthropic had agreed to spend $45 billion to rent AI cloud computing capacity from Nscale’s West Virginia data centre campus, while signing several similar deals with AWS, Google, etc.
The agreement gives Anthropic access to Akamai Cloud’s distributed infrastructure and software, with the focus initially on supporting its growing CPU workload requirements.

Anthropic’s growing AI infrastructure bill The Akamai agreement is part of a broader push by Anthropic to lock in the computing infrastructure required to train and operate increasingly capable AI models.
“Akamai has an unparalleled reputation for helping our customers achieve their business-critical goals and build the future.
The scale of Anthropic’s infrastructure requirements has been growing rapidly.

facts.text: Anthropic will spend $11.6 billion over seven years on Akamai’s cloud infrastructure, Akamai said Thursday .
That’s more than six times the size of a $1.8 billion deal between the two companies that Bloomberg reported in May.

As part of the deal, Akamai issued Anthropic a warrant, essentially the right to buy shares at a set price, for nonvoting preferred stock convertible into 7.7 million common shares, or up to about 5% of the company’s outstanding stock, at $111.33 a share.
About 2% is expected to vest, or become available to Anthropic once it makes its first payment under the deal.
It also represents a bet on a less-hyped corner of AI infrastructure: CPUs.

Demand for CPUs, the general-purpose chips that handle work like running code and browsing the web, has grown as AI agents take on more tasks, though Akamai didn’t say what Anthropic will use them for.
The warrant flips the more common pattern in circular AI deals , in which suppliers — chipmakers and cloud providers — invest directly in the AI labs that buy their products.
Here, the supplier is instead giving its customer a potential stake, one that grows as Anthropic’s spending with Akamai does.
AMD used a similar structure with OpenAI last year, tying warrants to chip-purchase milestones.
Akamai won’t see revenue from the deal this year.

On an investor call Thursday, executives said they expect $150 million to $300 million in 2027, starting in the second half, with revenue reaching an annual pace of about $1.7 billion by the end of 2028.
To build out the capacity, Akamai expects to spend about $5.5 billion.
Anthropic is no stranger to such arrangements.
Amazon , Google , Microsoft, and AMD have all invested or agreed to invest in the company while selling it chips or cloud capacity.
CEO Dario Amodei told The New York Times last December that Anthropic does not participate in these deals at the “same scale as some other players.”

sources.title: Google's first Suncatcher orbital data center test launches October 1
passages: Google is taking its first step toward making Project Suncatcher a reality.

Announced last year, Suncatcher is Google’s “moonshot” effort to design orbital AI data centers, which AI boosters like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos have pitched as an alternative to divisive terrestrial data centers .
Google’s first experimental satellite will launch on October 1 with the aim of validating Google’s vision for a constellation of AI satellites .
With this first test, Google hopes to understand what does and doesn’t work, allowing it to improve its designs for future missions.
The 2027 launches are still on the agenda, but the team expects it will be years before Suncatcher evolves from “project” to “product.”
Google’s experimental orbital data center will have four TPUs and only run for 15 minutes at a time.
Eventually, Google wants to have networks of orbiting satellites that communicate over high-speed laser connections, probably requiring expensive dedicated launches.
This lone satellite will serve as a test of several technologies and will operate for just a few months.
Cooling the chips may be the biggest issue , something many observers have pointed out as the AI industry has gone wild over the idea of orbital data centers.
Radiator systems exist in space, but they’re designed to remove a relatively small amount of heat.
AI accelerators generate far more heat by comparison.
Google’s solution uses a layer of malleable “thermal interface material” that connects the chips to aluminum and copper heat pipes.
Those components conduct heat into a radiator that can project it into space.
The satellite, dubbed MVP, is about the size of a refrigerator.
Inside, it has four of Google’s custom TPU AI accelerators, which are used to train AI models and run inference to generate tokens for AI workloads.
MVP is starting small, with solar panels that supply only about one kilowatt of power, The New York Times reports.
That’s enough to power a microwave or a hair dryer.
Google did not build the satellite from scratch.
The initial plan was to launch two custom satellites in 2027, but Google wanted to accelerate its efforts.
So the company opted to integrate its chips into a satellite that Planet Labs had already built for an early test.
Google will run Gemini models on the TPUs for testing, but they won’t be able to run continuously.
After that, the TPUs need to shut down to allow the radiators to catch up.
Google says it has conducted testing on the ground, but launching the satellite will provide a fuller picture of the current challenges.
For example, the team will need to evaluate how Tensor chips handle space conditions.
Radiation can damage chips or simply interfere with calculations by flipping bits.
But vibration and high g-forces during launch also pose problems.
Still, as we’ve seen with missions like the Ingenuity Mars helicopter , off-the-shelf hardware can hold up pretty well out there.

passages: Google is set to launch its first experimental satellite for “Project Suncatcher” on October 1, marking a significant step toward its goal of building orbital AI data centres powered by near-constant sunlight.
Experts caution the concept remains years from commercial viability due to high launch costs and engineering constraints.
Google stressed the first mission is about gathering data and recognising and identifying failure points, not showcasing an operational orbital data centre.
The satellite will run Gemini models for testing.
Future designs envision clusters of satellites carrying dozens of TPUs each, communicating via high-bandwidth lasers.
Google plans to launch two satellites in 2027 to test those laser links.
The refrigerator-sized satellite, named MVP, will carry four of Google’s custom Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission.
The spacecraft was built in partnership with satellite imagery firm Planet Labs.
The mission will assess how Google’s TPUs withstand launch forces, radiation, and thermal extremes.
Google said its Trillium TPUs held up well in ground tests, surviving radiation doses greater than what a five-year space mission would deliver.
In space, there’s no airflow; heat must be diffused via radiators.
Google’s design combines heat pipes and radiators, but the system can only run in roughly 15-minute bursts before the TPUs must shut down to let radiators catch up.

coreStoryFacts.text: Google is taking its first step toward making Project Suncatcher a reality.

Announced last year, Suncatcher is Google’s “moonshot” effort to design orbital AI data centers, which AI boosters like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos have pitched as an alternative to divisive terrestrial data centers .
Google’s first experimental satellite will launch on October 1 with the aim of validating Google’s vision for a constellation of AI satellites .
With this first test, Google hopes to understand what does and doesn’t work, allowing it to improve its designs for future missions.
The 2027 launches are still on the agenda, but the team expects it will be years before Suncatcher evolves from “project” to “product.”
Google’s experimental orbital data center will have four TPUs and only run for 15 minutes at a time.
Eventually, Google wants to have networks of orbiting satellites that communicate over high-speed laser connections, probably requiring expensive dedicated launches.
This lone satellite will serve as a test of several technologies and will operate for just a few months.
Cooling the chips may be the biggest issue , something many observers have pointed out as the AI industry has gone wild over the idea of orbital data centers.
Radiator systems exist in space, but they’re designed to remove a relatively small amount of heat.
AI accelerators generate far more heat by comparison.
Google’s solution uses a layer of malleable “thermal interface material” that connects the chips to aluminum and copper heat pipes.
Those components conduct heat into a radiator that can project it into space.
The satellite, dubbed MVP, is about the size of a refrigerator.
Inside, it has four of Google’s custom TPU AI accelerators, which are used to train AI models and run inference to generate tokens for AI workloads.
MVP is starting small, with solar panels that supply only about one kilowatt of power, The New York Times reports.
That’s enough to power a microwave or a hair dryer.
Google did not build the satellite from scratch.
The initial plan was to launch two custom satellites in 2027, but Google wanted to accelerate its efforts.
So the company opted to integrate its chips into a satellite that Planet Labs had already built for an early test.
Google will run Gemini models on the TPUs for testing, but they won’t be able to run continuously.
After that, the TPUs need to shut down to allow the radiators to catch up.
Google says it has conducted testing on the ground, but launching the satellite will provide a fuller picture of the current challenges.
For example, the team will need to evaluate how Tensor chips handle space conditions.

Google under Alphabet Inc. (GOOG) is preparing to launch its first experimental satellite as part of Project Suncatcher, an ambitious effort to develop AI data centers in orbit.
The spacecraft was built by Planet Labs, allowing Google to accelerate its testing rather than develop a satellite from scratch.

Google is set to launch its first experimental satellite for “Project Suncatcher” on October 1, marking a significant step toward its goal of building orbital AI data centres powered by near-constant sunlight.
Experts caution the concept remains years from commercial viability due to high launch costs and engineering constraints.
Google stressed the first mission is about gathering data and recognising and identifying failure points, not showcasing an operational orbital data centre.
The satellite will run Gemini models for testing.
Future designs envision clusters of satellites carrying dozens of TPUs each, communicating via high-bandwidth lasers.
Google plans to launch two satellites in 2027 to test those laser links.
The refrigerator-sized satellite, named MVP, will carry four of Google’s custom Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 as part of the Transporter-18 rideshare mission.
The spacecraft was built in partnership with satellite imagery firm Planet Labs.
The mission will assess how Google’s TPUs withstand launch forces, radiation, and thermal extremes.
Google said its Trillium TPUs held up well in ground tests, surviving radiation doses greater than what a five-year space mission would deliver.
In space, there’s no airflow; heat must be diffused via radiators.
Google’s design combines heat pipes and radiators, but the system can only run in roughly 15-minute bursts before the TPUs must shut down to let radiators catch up.

Announced last year, Suncatcher is Google’s “moonshot” effort to design orbital AI data centers, which AI boosters like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos have pitched as an alternative to divisive terrestrial data centers . Google’s first experimental satellite will launch on October 1 with the aim of validating Google’s vision for a constellation of AI satellites . The satellite, dubbed MVP, is about the size of a refrigerator. Inside, it has four of Google’s custom TPU AI accelerators, which are used to train AI models and run inference to generate tokens for AI workloads. On Earth, a data center will run thousands of these chips, which consume massive amounts of power—one of the reasons putting solar-powered AI hardware in space is so attractive. MVP is starting small, with solar panels that supply only about one kilowatt of power, The New York Times reports. That’s enough to power a microwave or a hair dryer. Google did not build the satellite from scratch. While the AI hardware inside is Google’s, the spacecraft comes from a satellite imagery firm called Planet Labs. The initial plan was to launch two custom satellites in 2027, but Google wanted to accelerate its efforts. So the company opted to integrate its chips into a satellite that Planet Labs had already built for an early test. Google’s AI test will launch as part of the upcoming Transporter-18 rideshare aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Eventually, Google wants to have networks of orbiting satellites that communicate over high-speed laser connections, probably requiring expensive dedicated launches. This lone satellite will serve as a test of several technologies and will operate for just a few months. Google says it has conducted testing on the ground, but launching the satellite will provide a fuller picture of the current challenges. For example, the team will need to evaluate how Tensor chips handle space conditions. In many space missions, hardware is designed specifically for extreme temperatures or radiation, but these are the same TPUs that Google integrates into servers on the ground. Radiation can damage chips or simply interfere with calculations by flipping bits. But vibration and high g-forces during launch also pose problems. Still, as we’ve seen with missions like the Ingenuity Mars helicopter , off-the-shelf hardware can hold up pretty well out there. Cooling the chips may be the biggest issue , something many observers have pointed out as the AI industry has gone wild over the idea of orbital data centers. Radiator systems exist in space, but they’re designed to remove a relatively small amount of heat. AI accelerators generate far more heat by comparison. Google’s solution uses a layer of malleable “thermal interface material” that connects the chips to aluminum and copper heat pipes. Those components conduct heat into a radiator that can project it into space. Google will run Gemini models on the TPUs for testing, but they won’t be able to run continuously. Google’s first experimental satellite will launch on October 1 with the aim of validating Google’s vision for a constellation of AI satellites .

The satellite, dubbed MVP, is about the size of a refrigerator. Inside, it has four of Google’s custom TPU AI accelerators, which are used to train AI models and run inference to generate tokens for AI workloads. On Earth, a data center will run thousands of these chips, which consume massive amounts of power—one of the reasons putting solar-powered AI hardware in space is so attractive.

MVP is starting small, with solar panels that supply only about one kilowatt of power, The New York Times reports. That’s enough to power a microwave or a hair dryer. Google did not build the satellite from scratch. While the AI hardware inside is Google’s, the spacecraft comes from a satellite imagery firm called Planet Labs. The initial plan was to launch two custom satellites in 2027, but Google wanted to accelerate its efforts. So the company opted to integrate its chips into a satellite that Planet Labs had already built for an early test.

Google’s AI test will launch as part of the upcoming Transporter-18 rideshare aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Eventually, Google wants to have networks of orbiting satellites that communicate over high-speed laser connections, probably requiring expensive dedicated launches. This lone satellite will serve as a test of several technologies and will operate for just a few months.

For example, the team will need to evaluate how Tensor chips handle space conditions. Still, as we’ve seen with missions like the Ingenuity Mars helicopter , off-the-shelf hardware can hold up pretty well out there.

Cooling the chips may be the biggest issue , something many observers have pointed out as the AI industry has gone wild over the idea of orbital data centers. Radiator systems exist in space, but they’re designed to remove a relatively small amount of heat. AI accelerators generate far more heat by comparison. Google’s solution uses a layer of malleable “thermal interface material” that connects the chips to aluminum and copper heat pipes. Those components conduct heat into a radiator that can project it into space.

Google will run Gemini models on the TPUs for testing, but they won’t be able to run continuously. The cooling system will only be able to operate in brief spurts of about 15 minutes. After that, the TPUs need to shut down to allow the radiators to catch up.

With this first test, Google hopes to understand what does and doesn’t work, allowing it to improve its designs for future missions. The 2027 launches are still on the agenda, but the team expects it will be years before Suncatcher evolves from “project” to “product.”

passages: When AI leaders at OpenAI and Anthropic started talking about “pacing the frontier,” maybe someone should have asked: what pace?
Now it’s turned into model drop week for both companies as Anthropic rolled out Opus 5.5 , followed by OpenAI’s GPT-6 model updates just 90 minutes later.

But the company that stole the spotlight was Meta, whose personal AI agent Muse is reportedly outpacing ChatGPT’s early numbers and is headed for smart glasses and a tiny Tamagotchi-style device next.

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Anthony Ha, and Sean O’Kane dig into Meta’s consumer AI strategy and what it means for the startups trying to build on top of this technology, covering everything from where the money is flowing to which AI products might actually become part of people’s daily lives.
They also get into a16z’s new school for aspiring founders and two very different AI and hardware deals.

But the company that stole the spotlight was Meta, whose personal AI agent Muse is reportedly outpacing ChatGPT’s early numbers and is headed for smart glasses and a tiny Tamagotchi-style device next. On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Anthony Ha, and Sean O’Kane dig into Meta’s consumer AI strategy and what it means for the startups trying to build on top of this technology, covering everything from where the money is flowing to which AI products might actually become part of people’s daily lives. They also get into a16z’s new school for aspiring founders and two very different AI and hardware deals.

passages: Meta has a new way to talk to its AI without putting on a pair of glasses.At the end of Wednesday's Meta Connect keynote, CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled Muse Charm, a small, always-on handheld device built around Muse, Meta's AI assistant.

extraction.body: Meta has a new way to talk to its AI without putting on a pair of glasses.At the end of Wednesday's Meta Connect keynote, CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled Muse Charm, a small, always-on handheld device built around Muse, Meta's AI assistant. The Tamagotchi-like gadget is designed for people who don't wear Meta's smart glasses, and Zuckerberg called it the fastest way to talk to Muse without wearing them. SEE ALSO: Meet the Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3, starting at $249 The reveal was set up earlier in the keynote. During a live demo, Zuckerberg used Meta's glasses to talk with his customized Muse assistant, which he'd named Agrippa, about a handheld device he was working on. That device turned out to be Muse Charm.Muse sat at the center of this year's keynote. Meta describes it as a personal agent that can set goals, share ideas, and run tasks in the background, and users can customize its personality and voice. Zuckerberg also suggested Meta could eventually collect a small fee on transactions the assistant helps complete.Muse Charm will ship by the holidays in December, according to Zuckerberg. Meta did not announce a price and said more details will come later.The device enters a category with a rocky track record. Standalone AI gadgets like Humane's Ai Pin and the Rabbit R1 drew harsh reviews after launching in 2024, and Humane discontinued the AI Pin the following year. Muse Charm's main selling point is that it runs on the same assistant as Meta's glasses.

sources.title: Meta’s Muse Charm Is a Tamagotchi-Style Puck for Its AI Agent, Shipping This December - Shane the Gamer
passages: Our take: Muse’s download numbers are real and worth paying attention to, but a keychain puck is a much harder sell than an app update.
Meta has form here, plenty of hardware side-bets from this company have quietly died within a year.
December will tell us whether Muse Charm ships as a real product or just as a Connect-stage tease that never gets a price tag.
On the official Connect blog, Meta kept the description brief, calling it “a delightful and fun device built for you to talk and interact with your Muse.”
Zuckerberg said it’s not finalized yet but that Meta is planning to have it ship “in time for the holidays” in December.
That timeline was echoed by outside coverage of the keynote, which likewise pegged the device to a holiday-season shipping window rather than a firm date or price.
Meta’s Muse app itself only launched on September 8 and has already had a genuinely strong run.
By the following week, Muse was the most popular free app in the iPhone’s App Store and had been downloaded more than 2.5 million times since launch.
Muse Charm was one piece of a wider push to get the agent off the phone screen entirely.
Meta says it is working to bring Muse to its AI glasses, extending the assistant from phones and computers to a device that can hear a request while its wearer is driving, cooking or exercising.

On glasses, Meta says Muse will be able to guide a personalized workout, log meals, offer nutrition information, help buy products a wearer sees, book appointments, check flight prices and search for replacement parts.
No price has been confirmed for Muse Charm, and Meta hasn’t detailed battery life, connectivity or whether it needs to pair with a phone to work.
The app is built to go further than a normal chatbot.
Muse already lets you shape that character before it ever reaches your keychain.
Zuckerberg demoed exactly that onstage, having reportedly named his own Muse Agrippa, a Roman figure mostly known for military successes.
That’s an ambitious list for a product line Meta itself frames as still in progress.
Meta has not disclosed a user count, revenue figure or product-specific budget for Muse, so the app store charts remain the only hard numbers available right now.
